label: Proposition G
title: Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park
q: Shall the City close Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4:00 a.m. through Friday at 6:00 p.m., unless a holiday falls on a weekday, in order to reopen the roadway known as the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles during that time?
now: Voters passed Proposition K in November 2024 with 54.73%, which closed the Upper Great Highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard to cars and made it a park. Cars came off on March 14, 2025. The road is now Sunset Dunes Park, closed to private vehicles at all times.${FS([21, 11, 54, 1])}
does: Closes the park from Monday 4 a.m. to Friday 6 p.m., except holidays, and reopens the road to private vehicles in those hours. The City must seek any Coastal Act permits this needs; the text sets no deadline and does not say what happens if a permit is refused.${FS([1, 9])}
yes: You want the road open to private vehicles on weekdays, and the park closed in those hours.${F(1)}
no: You don't want the City to make these changes.${F(1)}

y1.s: Supporters say it brings back the 2021 to 2025 arrangement: a park on weekends and holidays, a road on weekdays, and the paths east of the road open every day.
g: Westside families were promised a compromise and got a road closure.
This is the compromise that works for all and what good governance looks like.
the committee viewed the measure as allowing San Francisco to share the corridor rather than forcing an all-road or all-park choice.
Yes on G restores the compromise in place from 2021 to 2024
We had a compromise that worked. Out-of-touch politicians took it away. Prop G gives it back.
The previous compromise offered a practical balance: weekday vehicle access while maintaining recreational use at other times. And it worked.
We already had a compromise that worked.
Use what we own. Restore the compromise.
We urge you to restore the compromise
Prop G restores the compromise that already worked
Please vote YES on G to implement a fair and equitable compromise.
It gives San Franciscans recreational space on weekends and holidays while allowing the Great Highway to serve our transportation needs during the week.
Vote YES on Proposition G: The Compromise Worked
Prop G offers a fair balance: reopen the road to vehicles on weekdays and preserve recreational use on weekends.
San Francisco found a compromise that worked
Measure G is reasserting the communal agreement forged in compromise
Proposition G restores a smart solution where recreation and transportation coexist
Yes on G: A Compromise is Common Sense
src: "Yes on G restores the compromise in place from 2021 to 2024: it keeps the Great Highway closed on weekends, allowing access to it as a park, but opens it to vehicle travel Monday through Friday."
"The previous compromise offered a practical balance: weekday vehicle access while maintaining recreational use at other times. And it worked."
y1.fig: The weekend-only schedule ran for three and a half years, but the city never published the evaluation it planned, so whether it "worked" rests on the one 2021 study and the votes since. From August 2021 to March 14, 2025 the road was open to cars Monday 6 a.m. to Friday noon, 102 hours a week; Prop G opens it Monday 4 a.m. to Friday 6 p.m., 110 hours. Ordinance 258-22 counted "3,300 average daily weekend visits since August 2021". SFCTA wrote in 2021 that a timed closure "may be more useful as an interim step" but did not recommend it "for the long term because it has nearly all of the costs of the full promenade but only a portion of the potential benefits". In its opt-in survey of 3,989 people, 13% picked it, 53% full closure and 21% a four-lane road; the Outer Richmond (94121) leaned to a four-lane road (52%) and the Sunset ZIPs to full closure (52%). The Coastal Commission let the weekend-only pilot stand in May 2024, calling it "a public recreational access improvement". Changing the days or hours later would take another citywide vote.
resp: "Prop G is a park closure, not a compromise."

y2.s: Supporters say traffic injuries in Sunset neighborhoods rose sharply after the closure, and weekday access would take cars back off side streets.
g: Since the Great Highway closed, traffic injuries in Sunset neighborhoods have risen sharply
WE DON’T HAVE TO CHOOSE BETWEEN A GREAT PARK AND SAFE STREETS.
open to everyone on weekdays for commuting, school drop-offs, work trips, and emergency access
bringing more congestion, noise, pollution, and safety concerns to nearby families
weekday vehicle access that helps keep traffic off neighborhood streets
Frustrated drivers bail out to speed through residential streets
src: "Since the Great Highway closed, traffic injuries in Sunset neighborhoods have risen sharply – a serious and unacceptable threat to public safety."
"Allows weekday vehicle access on the Great Highway, helping keep traffic off neighborhood streets."
y2.fig: The crash data doesn't show the sharp rise supporters describe: District 4 had 96 injury crashes in the year before the closure (April to March) and 105 in the year after, inside its range of the years before (130 two years before), and Sunset Blvd went from 8 to 20 on small counts. Unverified. January to August 2026 is up 19% on 2025 (82 against 69), about the citywide rise of 15%. Calendar 2025 (99) was below 2019 (133) and 2024 (107). District 4 severe crashes went from 7 in 2024 to 14 in 2025, and were 15 in 2022 and 16 in 2020 with the road open on weekdays. Our own count of police reports, which doesn't yet match a published total. Unverified. Before the closure SFCTA counted "about 5 – 6" collisions a year on the Upper Great Highway, Lower Great Highway and La Playa, and warned that a full closure risked more collisions "on residential streets if pass through traffic is not diverted to larger arterials". Median fire and medical response in District 4 changed by seconds after the closure (6.35 minutes in April to August 2024, 6.43 in 2025), about the same as Districts 1 and 7. Our own query. Unverified. Supporters call the road "a critical coastal evacuation route" (finding 2(h)); DEM and SFFD wrote in February 2025 that it "is not a designated evacuation route".
resp: "Our streets are safer with Sunset Dunes. Analyzing public data, independent sources like The Frisc and Streetsblog agree: crashes in our neighborhood are down since the park opened."

Closing the Great Highway did not make traffic disappear. It simply pushed traffic onto other streets

src: "Closing the Great Highway did not make traffic disappear. It simply pushed traffic onto other streets, including residential streets never designed to carry the same volume of vehicles."
"Closing the Great Highway full time has made daily life harder for west‑side neighborhoods already underserved by transit."
y3.fig: The counts show traffic did move to other roads, and trips on them got somewhat slower; how much a weekday reopening would win back has not been studied. Before the closure the road carried 17,000 car trips a weekday in 2019, nearly two-thirds between the Richmond and the South Bay, and 14,471 vehicles a day in fall 2023. After it, Sunset Blvd carried 28% more traffic than in 2023 (about 90% of its 2019 level), Chain of Lakes about 21% more, and Lower Great Highway and Chain of Lakes about one more vehicle a minute at peak than before the pandemic. A year of city speed data shows southbound 19th Ave between Lincoln and Sloat 35 to 43 seconds slower at peak. The Chronicle measured the Outer Richmond to Zoo trip about 4.4 minutes longer in the morning rush, over a few weeks of data. SFCTA's 2021 model expected the road to carry up to 25% fewer cars once the extension south of Sloat closes. No study measures door-to-door trips, or delay for seniors, disabled residents or school trips.
resp: "Traffic fears have not materialized; three independent analyses confirm traffic impacts are minimal. The most impacted trips are 2-4 minutes longer during rush hour, with most trips unaffected."

y4.s: Supporters say Prop K closed the road without community meetings, over the votes of the Sunset and Richmond, and a citywide vote shouldn't override the neighborhoods that live with it.
g: The people most impacted (neighbors, commuters) voted overwhelmingly against closing the road.
many San Franciscans, including a majority of people in the Sunset District, have felt railroaded by the whole process.
adds to the feeling that this park is being imposed on Sunset residents by outsiders
This compromise was working until Sunset Supervisor Joel Engardio, without a single community meeting, put forward a measure permanently closing the Great Highway.
We organized because City Hall refused to listen.
To close a major roadway against the wishes of the great majority of its residents?
it was done without any regard for our neighborhood’s input
Politicians shouldn’t tell our communities what works when their plans keep failing us.
In 2024, nearly two‑third of westside residents voted to keep the road open because they depend on it.
a return to respecting the voices of neighborhoods
When City Hall failed to listen to impacted neighborhoods, nearly 16,000 San Franciscans signed the petition
I don’t think voters in one part of the City should make decisions that negatively affect another.
src: "This compromise was working until Sunset Supervisor Joel Engardio, without a single community meeting, put forward a measure permanently closing the Great Highway."
"In 2024, nearly two‑third of westside residents voted to keep the road open because they depend on it."
y4.fig: The vote records bear out the split: the two districts beside the road voted against Prop K while the city voted for it. Prop K passed 206,042 to 170,447 (54.73%) in November 2024; Districts 1 and 4 each voted about 64% against it, and the Outer Richmond about 71%. Supervisor Joel Engardio, who put Prop K on the ballot, was recalled in September 2025 with 62.72% at 43% turnout; the groups of precincts most against Prop K voted most for the recall (r = 0.95, our arithmetic), though that ballot asked about him, not the road. Prop G qualified by petition, which needed 10,615 valid signatures.
resp: "Voters already settled this. In November 2024, 55% of San Francisco approved Proposition K, permanently protecting Sunset Dunes park as open space and closing the former Upper Great Highway to cars."

y5.s: Supporters say most of the reopening cost is one-time signals, the road must be kept up anyway, and the permanent park has no price or funding.
g: lying atop the Westside Transport sewage aqueduct (which must be maintained regardless)
But the Controller says $8.8 million of that is for traffic signals at eight intersections – not removing the park.
a new road will not need to be built, financed or require extra upkeep
That’s a responsible use of public space and limited park resources
Now, with the Great Highway closed to vehicles 24/7, costs are going up, not down.
src: "Opponents cite a $9.8 million reopening price tag. But the Controller says $8.8 million of that is for traffic signals at eight intersections – not removing the park."
"Even the Controller acknowledges reopening would reduce weekday park staffing and maintenance needs, including approximately $300,000 in annual staffing costs."
y5.fig: No public document prices a permanent park, so the long-run cost of either choice can only be compared on running costs. The Controller puts park staffing at about $300,000 a year for 1.5 positions, which Prop G would partly save, and $8.8 million of the $9.8 million at signals. SFCTA's 2021 planning figures put yearly upkeep at $1,501,000 for a four-lane road, $1,593,000 for a full promenade and $2,088,600 for a weekend-only one, with road upkeep $200,000 with cars against $20,000 as a park and sand clearing $230,000 either way; those are another office's estimates from five years ago. So far about $913,000 of parks bond money and about $970,000 in private gifts, plus $90,000 in kind, have gone to interim features. Public Works sand spending was flat for a decade apart from the 2022-23 storm year. Rec and Park has no design, cost estimate or capital budget for a permanent park; in 2024 the Controller said a closed road "may result in increased trash pick-up, Park Ranger patrols or other operational costs", with no figure. ConnectedSF's $200 million is its own comparison with India Basin, a different park, and names no source. Unverified.
resp: "Proposition G asks you to spend nearly $10 million to demolish a coastal park (plus up to $1.9 million every year for added roadway maintenance)"

y6.s: Supporters say a car-free road shuts out people who can't walk or bike it, including disabled residents who were promised better access and still wait.
g: seniors, people with disabilities and others who rely on vehicles
no inclusion of the disabled, who best enjoy the scenic view as passengers
Disabled residents were promised better access. We are still waiting.
Families, workers, seniors, people with disabilities, cyclists, pedestrians, and drivers all deserve access to public land.
A 24/7 closure excludes people who rely on vehicles
src: "For 10 blocks along the Lower Great Highway between Judah and Taraval, there is not one ADA‑compliant point of access to Sunset Dunes from the Lower Great Highway."
"Real coastal accessibility must serve everyone, not just those who can stroll on a Tuesday morning."
y6.fig: Rec and Park's own assessment backs the entrance complaint: accessible entrances exist only at Lincoln, Judah, Taraval and Sloat, with one at Noriega planned for late 2026 to 2027. Once inside, the park is over 2 miles of flat paving, and one in four visitors who come with others brings a senior. Drivers can still see the coast from the Lower Great Highway and the Great Highway north of Lincoln, as the Coastal Commission noted.
resp: "Walking on a sandy beach is difficult or no longer an option for many seniors and people with disabilities, so we rely on Sunset Dunes park to enjoy the calm of a walk or roll by the ocean"

y7.s: Supporters say the city's visit counts are inflated because sensors count every pass, and that the road sat largely empty on weekdays.
g: The infrared sensors count every pass, so one person can be counted several times.
Yet it remains woefully underused Mon—Fri; and is practically devoid of people on rainy days.
src: "Yet it remains woefully underused Mon—Fri; and is practically devoid of people on rainy days."
y7.fig: The sensor counts do count passes rather than people, but they don't show the park empty on weekdays. Rec and Park counts "a visit ... every time a person passes infrared sensors": about 3,800 a weekday and 7,200 a weekend day in the first year, 53% on weekdays. How many sensors one person passes is not published, so visits overstate people by an unknown factor. GrowSF, which opposes G, estimates about 500,000 of the 1.7 million were new park use. A one-hour hand count at a weekday peak found 564 people moving past Noriega.
resp: "Nearly 60% of visits to Sunset Dunes are on weekdays."

y8.s: Supporters say the closure added detour miles, idling and neighborhood pollution, and that foot traffic over the dunes now damages plants and worsens erosion.
g: There has never been a formal environmental review of the project, which moved traffic into other environmentally sensitive areas.
That means additional vehicle miles traveled and emissions in residential neighborhoods.
bringing more congestion, noise, pollution, and safety concerns to nearby families
Diverting thousands of vehicles from an established route onto residential streets creates congestion, idling cars, and neighborhood pollution.
increased foot traffic over fragile dunes damages native plants, worsens erosion, and increases the need for costly dune reshaping
src: "Slower, less direct routes have environmental consequences. Vehicles travel farther and spend more time stopping, idling, and accelerating."

"Without traffic and pedestrian signals directing people to designated crossings, increased foot traffic over fragile dunes damages native plants, worsens erosion, and increases the need for costly dune reshaping."
y8.fig: Neither side's environmental claim has been measured. SFMTA counted 3,200 fewer vehicles a day across the two western park crossings and said those trips "may have shifted to 19th Avenue or to east-west roadways, changed mode of travel or are no longer taken", which fits either fewer miles driven or longer detours. No study of vehicle miles, air quality or dune damage since the closure was found.

y9.s: Supporters say weekday road access lets shoppers, deliveries and customers reach West Side shopping streets.
g: Prop G welcomes weekend park visitors while ensuring shoppers, deliveries, and local customers can reach our commercial corridors during the week.
src: "A thriving Westside needs year-round economic vitality. Prop G welcomes weekend park visitors while ensuring shoppers, deliveries, and local customers can reach our commercial corridors during the week."
y9.fig: No sales, sales-tax or foot-traffic data for West Side shopping streets were found for either side. The only figures are sales gains reported by businesses that signed the argument against.
resp: "Sunset Dunes became our neighborhood’s town square and has boosted local business revenue — some up to 50%."

src: "it would significantly increase the cost of government by approximately $9.8 million in one-time capital costs and by approximately $500,000 to $1.9 million annually."
"Proposition G asks you to spend nearly $10 million to demolish a coastal park (plus up to $1.9 million every year for added roadway maintenance)"
n1.fig: The official estimate is mostly signals up front and mostly sand each year, with some costs nobody has sized. One time: $8.8 million for new signals at 8 intersections, $750,000 to remove park elements and restore the road, $200,000 for striping and signs. Each year: sand and dune work $100,000 to $1.5 million more than now, while park staffing of about $300,000 would fall. The Controller also names costs it could not size: changes to the Ocean Beach project's planned plaza at Sloat, and coastal permit conditions "at a level that cannot be determined at this time". SFMTA told a reporter the old signals were past their useful life and would have cost about the same to restore had the road stayed open. South of Sloat the road is closing anyway, so a reopened road would end at Sloat. The alternative has no price yet: no public document costs a permanent park, and SFCTA's 2021 planning figures put yearly upkeep at $1,593,000 for a full promenade against $1,501,000 for a four-lane road.
resp: "And permanent closure wasn’t free." The Controller "says $8.8 million of that is for traffic signals at eight intersections – not removing the park", and "Even the Controller acknowledges reopening would reduce weekday park staffing and maintenance needs".

n2.fig: The features added since 2025 sit on the former roadway, but no document says which would be removed, and nobody has measured whether the paths beside the road could take the people who now use it. Rec and Park's July 2025 map puts the seating, art, exercise and nature areas, hammocks, bike track and skate space along the former roadway. The legal text names no park feature and orders no removal; the Controller budgets $750,000 to "remove existing park elements and restore roadway segments" and lists none. Rec and Park counted about 3,800 visits a weekday and 7,200 a weekend day in the first year, 53% on weekdays; a visit is each sensor pass. At one weekday peak hour its consultant counted 540 of 564 people (96%) on the former roadway, not the eastern path; one hour at one cross street. Open question: could the added features move beside the path? Unverified.
resp: "Sunset Dunes Park includes a paved 10′ wide 2‑mile long pedestrian path for walking or rolling, a jogging path, landscaping, many water fountains, park benches, and 2 bathrooms on the east side of the roadway. These amenities have always been there and will remain."

n3.t: An unreliable road on a moving coast
n3.s: Opponents say blowing sand closes the road without warning, Prop G sets no standard for clearing it, and keeping a road on the shore works against the city's climate plans.
g: would undo a successful city effort to protect neighborhoods from the threats of rising sea levels and coastal erosion
restore the dunes for wildlife and resilience to sea level rise
the Ocean Beach Master Plan, completed over a decade ago, concluded that keeping the highway in place could ultimately destroy the beach
the road often needed to be closed when it filled up with sand
Sunset Dunes is what coastal recovery looks like.
Sunset Dunes is the best plan for our coastal environment as we adapt to climate change and sea-level rise.
This eroding roadway closed unpredictably up to 65 days a year before Prop K
Proposition G blocks critically needed climate change adaptation to protect the Sunset against rising sea levels.
Meanwhile, the Great Highway closed up to 65 days each year due to sand accumulation, and the southern end is closing permanently.
an end to much‑needed coastal rehabilitation to prepare our coastline for the effects of climate change
src: "The roadway has been closed to vehicular traffic an average of 32 times each calendar year during the Pilot data collection period, with closures lasting anywhere from several hours to several days."
"Proposition G blocks critically needed climate change adaptation to protect the Sunset against rising sea levels."
n3.fig: Sand closures are frequent and can't be predicted, but the record doesn't show them or their cost rising, and official sources disagree about whether this stretch of shore is retreating. SFMTA and Rec and Park told the Board in 2024 that sand closed the road to cars "an average of 32 times each calendar year during the Pilot", with "no predictability"; that period fell mostly in the stormy winter of 2022-23. Prop G sets no service level for sand. The Controller expects sand and dune work to cost $100,000 to $1.5 million more a year, because a road for cars needs more clearing, not because sand is getting worse. Public Works spent $215,717 to $362,550 a year on sand from FY 2011 to FY 2022, then $759,054 in the 2022-23 storm year; the Controller's later years are $420,000, $290,000 and $330,000. On the shore: SFCTA wrote in 2021 that "the coastline continues to recede" and that a park "can be part of a managed retreat strategy", while USGS data cited by the Coastal Commission show the beach in front of the park growing about 4.3 feet a year from 2004 to 2020, with erosion and managed retreat south of Sloat. The Controller says signals at Sloat would change the Ocean Beach Climate Change Adaptation Project's planned plaza, at an added cost it couldn't size.
resp: "Sand maintenance is regularly occurring to keep what once was the Upper Great Highway open for use by City and emergency vehicles 24/7"

n4.s: Opponents point to Proposition K, which voters passed in 2024, and say a third citywide vote on the same road should not undo it.
g: San Francisco has voted on this twice.
should be given the chance to keep succeeding
reverting what SF voters already decided
our signature thresholds are too low
you voted for this in 2022 and 2024 already. just vote no again
we are not supportive of the process of continuing to re-litigate issues through ballot measures
San Francisco voters will decide for the third time in four years what to do with the Great Highway.
San Franciscans have weighed in on this stretch of coastline again and again.
src: "Voters already settled this. In November 2024, 55% of San Francisco approved Proposition K, permanently protecting Sunset Dunes park as open space and closing the former Upper Great Highway to cars."
"Six years of debate, two citywide votes, two lawsuits, three appeals. Enough is enough"
n4.fig: Voters have decided twice, and Prop G qualified the way any petition does. Prop K passed 206,042 to 170,447 (54.73%) in November 2024. Prop G rewrites the Park Code section Prop K wrote and strikes its "at all times" rule. It qualified by petition, which needed 10,615 valid signatures, 2% of registered voters. GrowSF says voters also rejected a 2022 measure to keep cars on the road, "65% to 35%". Unverified.
resp: "In 2024, nearly two‑third of westside residents voted to keep the road open because they depend on it."

n5.s: Opponents say drivers found other routes, the worst trips are a few minutes longer at rush hour, and a road won't fix congestion anyway.
g: the promise that highway expansion will solve congestion has proved false over and over again for decades
roughly three minutes of peak-hour travel time on weekdays
no statistically significant changes to congestion and collision rates
the carmageddon the opponents of the park said would happen as a result
Traffic fears have not materialized; three independent analyses confirm traffic impacts are minimal.
Traffic fears raised two years ago haven’t materialized.
There is no traffic reason to close Sunset Dunes park.
Traffic is fine, and we can still get everywhere we need to go.
the studies confirm impacts are limited to 2-4 minutes at rush hour
src: "Traffic fears have not materialized; three independent analyses confirm traffic impacts are minimal. The most impacted trips are 2-4 minutes longer during rush hour, with most trips unaffected."
n5.fig: The displaced drivers are measured: they moved onto other roads, which got somewhat busier and slower, within what the city's model predicted. Sunset Blvd carried 28% more traffic than in 2023, Chain of Lakes about 21% more, and Chain of Lakes and Lower Great Highway about one more vehicle a minute at peak than before the pandemic. Southbound 19th Ave between Lincoln and Sloat is 35 to 43 seconds slower at peak over a year of city speed data, and the Outer Richmond to Zoo trip about 4.4 minutes longer in the Chronicle's few weeks of data. Two of the "three independent analyses" are news analyses and the third is by SFMTA, which carried out the closure. See "Losing the park" for the other displacement claim, where park users would go, which has no such measure.
resp: "Closing the Great Highway did not make traffic disappear. It simply pushed traffic onto other streets, including residential streets never designed to carry the same volume of vehicles."

n6.s: Opponents say crashes in the Sunset fell after the park opened, so safety is no reason to reopen the road.
g: City data refutes claims that traffic injuries rose in the Sunset since the Great Highway closed.
no statistically significant changes to congestion and collision rates
crashes in our neighborhood are down since the park opened
Car crashes are down in the neighborhood since the park opened
injury collisions on D4 streets dropped below 2019 and 2024 levels
crashes in the Sunset are down
src: "Our streets are safer with Sunset Dunes. Analyzing public data, independent sources like The Frisc and Streetsblog agree: crashes in our neighborhood are down since the park opened."
n6.fig: The crash data doesn't clearly show a fall either: District 4 had 96 injury crashes the year before the closure and 105 the year after, and calendar 2025 (99) was below 2019 (133) and 2024 (107), so the sign depends on the window picked. January to August 2026 rose 19%, close to the citywide 15%, and Sunset Blvd went from 8 to 20. Our own count of police reports. Unverified.
resp: "Since the Great Highway closed, traffic injuries in Sunset neighborhoods have risen sharply – a serious and unacceptable threat to public safety."

n7.s: Opponents say the park is a rare place to walk, roll and bike without traffic, including the Sunset's only protected north-south bike route.
g: We need more meaningful spaces where we can walk without fear of dangerous vehicle traffic, not fewer.
would remove the only protected, north-south bike route in the Sunset Districts
A whole generation of SF kids is learning to ride their bikes out there
teach our kids to bike and scoot
Sunset Dunes park is now a place for people of all ages, especially seniors and children, to walk without fear.
This is why it’s critical to have safe spaces like Sunset Dunes park for people of all ages and abilities to be without the threat of dangerous traffic.
src: "Every 15 hours on average, someone suffers serious injuries in a traffic crash and is rushed to San Francisco General Hospital."
"This is why it’s critical to have safe spaces like Sunset Dunes park for people of all ages and abilities to be without the threat of dangerous traffic."
n7.fig: Under Prop G the park would be car-free on weekends and holidays and the paths east of the road would stay open every day. Before the closure SFCTA found no pedestrian or bicycle deaths on the Upper Great Highway. SF Bike's "only protected, north-south bike route" was not checked. Unverified.
resp: "Bicyclists have always had safe 24/7 access whether or not private vehicles shared the road."

n8.s: Opponents say weekday cars would end dune restoration, disturb shorebirds and bring exhaust and runoff back to the coast.
g: A dune system cannot be restored two days a week.
restore the dunes for wildlife and resilience to sea level rise
There are real ecological benefits to closing this space to cars, including the decreased pollution, noise and artificial lighting
bring back the vehicular pollution we just got rid of
Proposition G replaces progress with pollution.
increase pollution runoff into a sensitive coastal ecosystem
Proposition G dumps automobile pollution into our sensitive coastal habitat.
src: "Proposition G erases our environmental gains. Dune restoration is underway, and local awareness and stewardship of our threatened Western Snowy Plover is increasing."
n8.fig: The Coastal Commission credited the closure with ecological benefit, but no one has measured the habitat, emissions or runoff since. In December 2024 it cited a San Francisco Estuary Institute report describing closure as having the "greatest and most immediate ecological benefits", and credited reduced driving and greenhouse gases. No measurement of dune recovery, plover numbers, air quality or runoff since March 2025 was found. The city's climate plan calls for dune work by 2029 to reduce erosion and blowing sand.
resp: "increased foot traffic over fragile dunes damages native plants, worsens erosion, and increases the need for costly dune reshaping"

n9.s: Opponents say Prop G writes the hours into law, so the Board couldn't adjust them and any change would take another citywide vote.
g: move the Friday closing back to noon, where the old compromise had it
Proposition G locks our coast into being a road forever.
src: "Proposition G locks our coast into being a road forever. Community planning is underway to transform the coast into a world-class park, but Proposition G kills all future park improvements."
n9.fig: The legal text does fix the days and hours. The Board may change technical details with 8 votes, but the days and hours need a public vote. No document explains why Prop G chose 6 p.m. Friday and 4 a.m. Monday rather than the old noon Friday and 6 a.m. Monday.
resp: "Maintains the whole space as a park on weekends and holidays."

n10.s: Opponents say the park brought customers to Outer Sunset shops, and closing it on weekdays would cost them most of those visitors.
g: the park is popular and benefiting nearby businesses
hurt the local businesses that are patronized by park visitors
Sunset Dunes became our neighborhood’s town square and has boosted local business revenue
Closing the park would harm the Sunset’s small businesses, removing tens of thousands of customers from our doorsteps every week.
src: "Andytown Coffee Roasters’s revenue is up 15–20% across its three Outer Sunset locations."
"Black Bird Bookstore & Cafe’s sales are up 44%"
n10.fig: The only figures are the businesses' own, from businesses that signed the argument; no sales-tax or foot-traffic data were found. Business registrations near the park show neither a surge of openings nor a wave of closures.
resp: "Prop G welcomes weekend park visitors while ensuring shoppers, deliveries, and local customers can reach our commercial corridors during the week."

n11.s: Opponents say the car-free promenade lets seniors, wheelchair users and families reach the ocean when sand is too hard to walk on.
g: Closing this park would take away an incredible open space for San Francisco residents, seniors, and families.
Our city’s coast belongs to all San Franciscans, not just the lucky few who live near it.
The park’s promenade, seating, and picnic tables let older people with mobility issues easily stroll with a walker and roll in a wheelchair
For many in our community who rely on mobility aids or can no longer walk through uneven sand, they rely on the park
Voting NO on Proposition G keeps our coast accessible to everyone, every day of the week.
src: "Walking on a sandy beach is difficult or no longer an option for many seniors and people with disabilities, so we rely on Sunset Dunes park to enjoy the calm of a walk or roll by the ocean"
n11.fig: Both sides' access claims hold at once: the park is over 2 miles of flat paving, and most of its entrances aren't accessible. Rec and Park lists accessible entrances only at Lincoln, Judah, Taraval and Sloat, and one in four visitors who come with others brings a senior. Its consultant perceived over 15% of Thursday walkers as 65 or older.
resp: "Disabled residents were promised better access. We are still waiting."

n12.s: Opponents say the city already gives most of its street space to cars, and one stretch of coast should go to people instead.
g: so drivers get to dominate 46 north-south roads in the Sunset District, including Sunset Boulevard, instead of 45?
this is in line with the city's 2021 Climate Action Plan, which recommends decreasing space dedicated to cars
Only 3% of SF streets have separated bike lanes
We should be advocating for more parks - not trying to close them down.
We need more meaningful spaces where we can walk without fear of dangerous vehicle traffic, not fewer.
we choose the Panhandle over highways
src: "We’ve made this choice before: San Francisco would never vote to destroy parks to rebuild the Embarcadero or Central freeways, and we choose the Panhandle over highways."
n12.fig: The figures here are the guides' own and weren't checked against city street data. Streetsblog counts 45 north-south roads in the Sunset besides this one, and the SF Bicycle Coalition says only 3% of city streets have separated bike lanes. Unverified. The Coastal Commission found the full closure "helps to maximize public recreational access".
resp: "The Great Highway belongs to everyone — not just bicyclists, skateboarders, and health-conscious people."

y1: SFCTA called a timed closure a possible interim step, not a long-term answer, and in its opt-in survey 13% picked it. The Coastal Commission let the weekend-only pilot stand in May 2024 as an access improvement.
y2: Our unverified count of police reports shows District 4 injury crashes at 96 the year before the closure and 105 the year after, against 130 two years before, while Sunset Blvd went from 8 to 20. Before the closure SFCTA counted about 5 to 6 collisions a year on the Great Highway and warned that a full closure risked more on residential streets.
y3: Sunset Blvd traffic rose 28% over 2023, and city speed data show southbound 19th Ave 35 to 43 seconds slower at peak. Opponents' answer, that traffic moved and it's fine, is the other side of the same displacement question as "Losing the park".
y4: Districts 1 and 4 each voted about 64% against Prop K, which passed with 54.73% citywide. District 4 recalled Supervisor Engardio with 62.72% at 43% turnout, on a ballot about him rather than the road.
y5: SFCTA's 2021 figures put yearly upkeep at $1.50 million for a road, $1.59 million for a full promenade and $2.09 million for a weekend-only one. No one has priced a permanent park; about $913,000 of bond money and $970,000 in gifts have gone to interim features.
y6: Accessible entrances exist only at Lincoln, Judah, Taraval and Sloat; one at Noriega is funded for late 2026 to 2027. The paved surface inside is over 2 miles long and flat.
y7: A visit is each pass of an infrared sensor, so one person can count more than once. The first year averaged about 3,800 visits a weekday and 7,200 a weekend day.
y8: SFMTA counted 3,200 fewer vehicles a day across the western park crossings, which may mean shorter or longer trips. No emissions or dune study since the closure was found.
y9: No sales or foot-traffic data for West Side shops were found. The only figures are from businesses that signed the argument against.
y10: No study of rents near the park since the closure was found. The claim comes from one paid argument and guides that took no position.
n1: $8.8 million is for signals at 8 intersections and $750,000 to remove park elements and restore the road; sand work adds $100,000 to $1.5 million a year and park staffing of about $300,000 would fall. For the park, no permanent design or cost exists; SFCTA's 2021 estimate of yearly upkeep was $1.59 million as a full promenade against $1.50 million as a road, and about $913,000 in bond money and $970,000 in gifts have gone to interim features.
n2: The features added since 2025 sit along the former roadway on Rec and Park's map; the paths, restrooms and fountains east of it predate the park, and supporters say Prop G "Retains access to walking paths, bike lanes, and all off-road amenities". Drivers who moved have counts behind them (Sunset Blvd +28%, 19th Ave 35 to 43 seconds slower), while nothing measures how many park users the paths could hold or where the features could go.
n3: Sand closed the road about 32 times a year during the pilot, at unpredictable times, and sand spending was flat for a decade apart from the 2022-23 storm year. USGS data show the beach in front of the park growing; erosion and managed retreat are south of Sloat.
n4: Prop K passed with 54.73% citywide in 2024. Prop G qualified by petition with at least 10,615 valid signatures.
n5: Sunset Blvd carried 28% more traffic and Chain of Lakes about 21% more, and 19th Ave southbound was 35 to 43 seconds slower at peak. This is the measured half of the displacement question; where park users would go under "Losing the park" has no measure.
n6: District 4 went from 96 injury crashes to 105 across the closure, but calendar 2025 was below 2019 and 2024. Which window is picked decides the sign; these are our own unverified counts.
n7: Under Prop G the paths east of the road stay open daily and the road is car-free on weekends and holidays. SFCTA found no pedestrian or bicycle deaths on the Upper Great Highway before the closure.
n8: The Coastal Commission credited the closure with ecological benefit in December 2024. No measurement of dunes, birds or pollution since was found.
n9: The Board may change technical details with 8 votes, but the days and hours need a citywide vote. No document explains the 6 p.m. Friday and 4 a.m. Monday times.
n10: The sales gains are reported by businesses that signed the argument. No independent sales data were found.
n11: The park's surface is flat and paved, but accessible entrances exist only at four streets. One in four visitors who come with others brings a senior.
n12: The road and bike-lane counts are the guides' own. The Coastal Commission found the full closure maximizes public recreational access.
